name: King's Indian: Classical
summary: The Classical King's Indian (5.Nf3 O-O 6.Be2 e5) pits Black's ...f5 kingside pawn storm against White's queenside play with the c5 break.
intro: The Classical Variation is the traditional main line of the King's Indian Defence, reached after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Be2 e5. White completes a natural, full-blooded classical setup with Nf3, Be2 and short castling, while Black fianchettoes, castles and stakes a claim in the centre with 6...e5. From here the game usually forks between two very different worlds. If White closes the centre with d5, the position becomes a race: Black attacks on the kingside with ...f5, ...f4 and ...g5, sending a pawn avalanche at White's king, while White expands on the queenside with c5 and pressure down the c-file. If White instead releases the tension with dxe5, the game takes on a quieter, more manoeuvring character. It is one of the sharpest and most double-edged battles in all of opening theory.

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The heart of the Classical King's Indian is the central pawn tension between White's d4 and e4 and Black's d6 and e5. Black's whole strategy is built around the fianchettoed g7-bishop and the readiness to expand on whichever wing the structure dictates. When White plays d5 and closes the centre, the position acquires a fixed pawn chain, with White's pawns pointing at the queenside and Black's at the kingside, and each side attacks in the direction their chain points. Knights reroute to their ideal squares: Black often plays ...Ne8 or ...Nd7 to clear the f-pawn, while White manoeuvres a knight to d3 to support c5 and blockade.

The resulting middlegame is a pure race. Black throws the kingside pawns forward with ...f5, ...f4, ...g5, ...h5 and ...g4, prising open lines against White's king, and will happily sacrifice material for the attack. White counters on the other flank, breaking with c5, opening the c-file and infiltrating on the queenside, often aiming to promote a passed pawn or crash through before Black's assault arrives. Whoever is faster usually wins outright, which gives the line its fearsome reputation. If instead the centre is opened early with dxe5, the play is more balanced and positional, revolving around control of the d-file and the d4- and d5-squares rather than mutual attacks.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 6...e5 the whole game hinges on White's response to the central tension. The most critical try is 7.O-O Nc6 8.d5 Ne7, the famous Mar del Plata main line, where the centre locks and both sides race: Black continues with ...Ne8 or ...Nd7, ...f5 and ...f4 and a kingside pawn storm, while White plays c5, opens the c-file and pushes on the queenside. These positions are among the most deeply analysed in the entire King's Indian and have produced some of its most spectacular attacking games.

White has several important alternatives that avoid the mutual mating race. The Petrosian System, 7.d5 followed by Bg5, closes the centre at once and steers play toward a more strategic struggle in which the knight reroutes to d7 and Black seeks ...a5 or a later ...f5. The Gligorić Variation, 7.Be3, keeps the tension and pressures e5, inviting ...Ng4 with concrete play. The Exchange Variation, 7.dxe5 dxe5 8.Qxd8 Rxd8, heads for a queenless middlegame that is drier but far from lifeless, with White pressing on the d-file and the light squares.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The King's Indian Defence took its modern shape in the 1930s and 1940s, when a generation of Soviet players demonstrated that Black could allow a big centre and then counterattack it dynamically. The Classical Variation, with White's natural Nf3 and Be2 development, became the principal main line and the proving ground for the opening's ideas.

It grew into the signature weapon of some of the greatest attacking players in history. Mikhail Tal, Bobby Fischer and above all Garry Kasparov used the King's Indian to devastating effect, and specialists such as Efim Geller, Svetozar Gligorić, after whom the 7.Be3 line is named, and later Teimour Radjabov and Hikaru Nakamura kept it at the top of the game. The Classical remains the benchmark against which every King's Indian repertoire is measured, prized for its uncompromising, fighting character.
